Aciclovir is given for CNS infec- tions and disseminated HSV infections,1,6,20 with fo- scarnet or cidofovir as alternatives for infections resist- ant to aciclovir.6 Neonates with evidence of herpes infection should be given high-dose intravenous aciclo- vir.7,9,20 Immunocompromised patients with frequent or disabling recurrences may benefit from prophylactic oral aciclovir or famciclovir.6,20,21 Prevention. Intravenous aciclovir is recommended for all HSV-seropositive patients undergoing allogeneic haemat- opoietic stem cell transplants to prevent reactivation of la- tent HSV. Aciclovir may also be considered for HSV-sero- positive patients undergoing autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation who are at risk of developing se- vere mucositis from the conditioning chemotherapy.22 Oral aciclovir, famciclovir, or valaciclovir may be given to patients who can tolerate oral therapy. There is a risk of neonatal herpes in the infants of mothers with genital her- pes infection. Prophylactic use of aciclovir in late pregnan- cy is not routinely recommended7 but may be considered in HIV-infected mothers with frequent recurrences.21 Al- though antivirals reduce viral shedding and recurrence at labour and birth and the use of caesarean section there is no evidence they reduce the occurrence of neonatal her- pes.23 1.
